name: Unwinding lots from either end
brief:
A position is held as a queue of lots, and `lots[i]` is the size of lot `i`. A trader may close lots only from the front or the back of the queue, one at a time. The closed lots must add up to exactly `x`.

Write `fewest_end_lots(lots, x)`, which returns the fewest lots to close, or -1 when no choice of ends adds up to `x`.

Example. For `lots = [3, 1, 4, 2, 2]` and `x = 5`, closing 3 from the front and 2 from the back takes 2 lots. Closing the last two lots and the 1 is not allowed, since the 1 is not at an end. The answer is 2.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 200{,}000$ lots, each a whole number from $1$ to $10^4$; $0 \le x \le 2 \cdot 10^9$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Trying every split between front and back is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: The lots left open form one unbroken middle stretch that adds up to `sum(lots) - x`. Find the longest such stretch with a sliding window.

examples.note: The middle 1, 4, 2 stays open, so 2 lots close.
Every choice of ends adds up to 0, 5 or 10, never 3.

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method tries every number of lots from the front and searches for the rest at the back, which is quadratic and runs out of time on the large tests. The step to the target is to turn the question round: the open lots are one middle stretch, so find the longest stretch that adds up to `sum(lots) - x`.
notes: Closing from both ends leaves one unbroken middle stretch, so fewest closed means longest stretch adding to `sum(lots) - x`.
When `x` is the whole sum the stretch is empty, and when `x` is more than the sum there is no answer at all.
Lots are positive, so the window sum rises and falls with its edges; each lot enters and leaves once, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: Always closing the larger end is a greedy that can overshoot when a smaller lot was needed.
Returning the length of the open stretch answers how many lots stay, not how many close.
Trying every front count and scanning the back each time is right but quadratic, so the large tests run out of time.
